title: The Binomial Distribution
quickIdea: Count the successes in a fixed number of independent trials with a constant success probability: P(X = k) = C(n,k) p^k (1-p)^(n-k), with mean np and variance np(1-p).
remember: The four conditions, all of which must hold: a fixed number n of trials, exactly two outcomes per trial, the same p in every trial, and independence between trials.
PMF: P(X = k) = C(n,k) p^k (1 - p)^(n-k) for k = 0, 1, ..., n. Mean np, variance np(1 - p), standard deviation sqrt(np(1-p)).
The single Bernoulli trial is the case n = 1, with mean p and variance p(1-p).
Sampling without replacement from a finite population breaks the constant-p condition: the counts are then hypergeometric, not binomial. The binomial is the with-replacement model.
'At least one' is almost always faster by complement: P(X >= 1) = 1 - (1-p)^n.
When n is large and p is small with np moderate, the binomial is well approximated by a Poisson with lambda = np; this is the bridge between the two cards.

example.prompt: A set has 2n elements and an unbiased coin is tossed for each. An element is chosen when its toss is a head. What is the probability that exactly n elements are chosen?
example.work: The number of chosen elements is a binomial variable with n_trials = 2n and p = 1/2. So P(X = n) = C(2n, n) (1/2)^n (1/2)^n = C(2n, n)/4^n. For n = 5 the value is 252/1024 = 0.2461.
example.answer: C(2n, n)/4^n, which is 0.2461 at n = 5.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2006 Q.21 is this question, and the options are built from the two mistakes: dividing by 2^n instead of 4^n, and inverting the fraction. The count C(2n, n) is the number of ways to choose which n of the 2n tosses are heads, and 4^n is the total number of toss sequences - the two ingredients of every binomial computation.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2006 Q.21: for each element of a set of size 2n an unbiased coin is tossed independently, and the element is chosen on a head. The probability that exactly n elements are chosen is (A) C(2n,n)/4^n (B) C(2n,n)/2^n (C) 1/C(2n,n) (D) 1/2.
variations.why: Binomial with 2n trials and p = 1/2: the count of favourable sequences is C(2n,n) and each sequence has probability (1/2)^(2n) = 1/4^n. Option (D) is the tempting 'half the elements' answer, which is the mean divided by 2n, not a probability of an exact count.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: A coin with P(head) = 0.4 is tossed 10 times. Find the probability of exactly 3 heads and the mean and variance of the count.
variations.why: C(10,3) = 120, and 120 x 0.064 x 0.02799 = 0.2150. The mean is np = 4 and the variance np(1-p) = 2.4, so the standard deviation is 1.549 - which is the quantity GATE asked for in 2024 Set 2 Q.8.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why is drawing 5 bulbs without replacement from a box of 20 containing 4 defectives not a binomial experiment?
variations.answer: Because the probability of a defective changes after each draw, so p is not constant across trials.
variations.why: The first draw is defective with probability 4/20; if it is defective, the second is defective with probability 3/19. Only with replacement would p stay at 1/5 and the count be binomial; without replacement the count is hypergeometric.

trap.what: Using the binomial when p changes between trials, or forgetting the binomial coefficient.
trap.why: The coefficient counts the orderings of the successes; without it you have the probability of one specific sequence, not of the count.
trap.counterexample: P(exactly 3 heads in 10 tosses) = C(10,3)/1024 = 0.1172, whereas the probability of one particular sequence with 3 heads and 7 tails is 1/1024 = 0.001. Dropping the coefficient is off by a factor of 120.

check.question: A fair coin is tossed 6 times. What is the probability of at least one head?
check.explanation: By the complement, P(at least one head) = 1 - P(no heads) = 1 - (1/2)^6 = 63/64. Summing the binomial probabilities for k = 1 to 6 gives the same number and takes six times as long.
